title: PixelVLA: Pixel-Level Robot Vision
one_liner: Add pixel-level target identification so robots can learn from where a human points, not just from text.
lead: Vision-language-action models teach robots to manipulate objects by learning from images and language instructions. But they fail at fine-grained tasks because they work at the image level, not the pixel level — they see the whole scene and guess at the details. PixelVLA adds a second processing path that zooms into specific pixels, so the robot can learn from visual prompts when a human points or draws a box to show what to manipulate.

problem.h2: Robots trained from images alone miss fine details
paras: Today's robot models learn to pick up objects by reading a camera image and a text instruction like 'grab the small red block.' But they miss the exact pixels the human meant—they process the whole image as a blurry summary, so they cannot see where the human is pointing.

A beginner would try to make the image clearer or give more examples, but that does not work, because the model itself has no way to convert a human's point or box into an action. There is no link from 'pixel coordinates' to 'arm movement.'

callout.html: Add a second processing path that extracts information from specific pixels where a human points, so the robot can learn to act on those exact locations.

steps.b: Extract image features at multiple scales
steps.text: A vision model (DinoV2) reads the image at different zoom levels.

steps.b: Create a pixel mask from the human input
steps.text: Convert the human's point or box into a binary mask: 1 for pixels in the pointed region, 0 for pixels elsewhere.

steps.b: Amplify features where the mask is 1
steps.text: Multiply each pixel-level feature by the mask; only pointed pixels survive.

steps.b: Feed the amplified features to the language model
steps.text: Combine these pixel-level summaries (the numbers extracted from the pointed region) with the language instruction before predicting the action.

steps.b: Train on image-text-action triples with pixel labels
steps.text: Use actual robot trajectories where humans marked the pixels involved in each action.

paras: A robot model processes images in two stages. In stage one, it learns continuous arm movements from a large mix of image-text-action data, like today's models. In stage two, it adds two new components: a pixel-aware encoder and a prompt-aware encoder. The pixel-aware encoder extracts and amplifies information from the specific pixels a human marked; the prompt-aware encoder converts the human's point or box into spatial coordinates the model can use.

hidden.h2: The key quantity: pixel-level signal strength
hidden.name: Pixel-level signal strength in the model
paras: A pixel-aware embedding (a numerical summary, a list of numbers the model creates) shows how much useful information the model extracted from a specific region of the image. High values in the embedding mean the model found strong, clear features in that region; low values mean the region looks like empty space to the model.

PixelVLA measures this by taking the multi-scale image features (extracted at different zoom levels) and multiplying them by a mask (1 where the human pointed, 0 elsewhere). Only the features in the pointed region survive; their sum forms the pixel-aware embedding. The paper's key move is: during training on this new pixel-level dataset, the model learns to connect these region-specific embeddings directly to robot actions.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger signal. Green boxes: human-marked pixels (input), model summary (middle), action output (result).

reads.html: The pixel-aware embedding is a list of numbers (a vector, just numbers in a row) that summarizes what the model sees in the pointed region. Bigger numbers mean the model found clearer, more useful information in that region.

The pixel-aware embedding is computed by taking features at each zoom level, zeroing out all pixels except the pointed ones, and summing the results. Then a small neural network (an MLP) remaps these summed numbers.

mechanism.h2: Why pixel-level prompts teach the robot better
paras: When a robot learns from text alone ('grab the red block'), the model has no way to know which red block in a cluttered scene, or even where in the image to look. The instruction is ambiguous. A human's visual prompt (a point, a box, a line) removes that ambiguity by saying 'look exactly here.'

PixelVLA extracts features specifically from the pointed pixels and feeds them directly into the model's decision-making core (the language model backbone). This gives the model a tight causal link: these specific pixels lead to this action. Because the pixel features are so precise, the model does not waste training effort on irrelevant regions and can learn faster and more accurately. The two-stage training ensures the pixel path does not interfere with the general motion knowledge the model already learned in stage one.

stages.s: DinoV2 extracts features at three zoom levels
Multiply features by mask to isolate signal
Merge pixel embeddings with text via language model
Robot action: arm position, gripper grip

math.words: Pixel-aware embedding equals the sum over all image scales of (the features at that scale, masked and projected). In words: for each zoom level of the image, keep only the pixels the human marked, project those features, and add them all up.
math.equation: E_p = MLP(sum_i Gamma_i(f_masked_i)) where f_masked_i = p * f_i, p is the pixel mask, f_i are features at scale i, Gamma_i is a linear projection for scale i
symbols: the pixel-aware embedding (output list of numbers for the robot to use)
the pixel mask (1 where human pointed, 0 elsewhere)
features extracted at zoom level i
a linear projection (matrix multiply) that maps scale i features to a common dimension
a small neural network (multilayer perceptron) that remaps the summed features

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose we have 2 zoom levels. Scale 1 (zoomed out) has features [4, 6, 2]. Scale 2 (zoomed in) has features [7, 1, 5].
The human points to a box; the mask is [1, 1, 0] (all 3 region pixels, all not in box).
Project scale 1: Gamma_1([4, 6, 0]) = [4, 6, 0] (assume identity for example). Project scale 2: Gamma_2([7, 1, 0]) = [7, 1, 0].
Sum: [4, 6, 0] + [7, 1, 0] = [11, 7, 0] (high values in first two positions, where human pointed; zero in third, where masked out).
Pass through MLP: [11, 7, 0] becomes the pixel-aware embedding, e.g., [2.1, 1.8, 0.3] after remapping. The robot uses this to decide the arm move.

math.note: The mask (1 or 0 at each pixel) is a filter: only features in the pointed region survive (multiply by 1); features outside are zeroed (multiply by 0). The surviving features form the embedding.

charts.title: Without pixel prompts (text-only baseline)
charts.note: Text instructions are ambiguous in complex scenes; the model guesses and fails.

charts.title: With PixelVLA (pixel-level training)
charts.note: Visual prompts resolve ambiguity; the model learns sharp pixel-to-action links, especially in hard cases.

items.html: If the human's point or bounding box is inaccurate (off by a few pixels or marking the wrong object), the pixel-aware encoder receives bad signal and can mislead training. The robot learns to act on the wrong region.

items.b: Pixel region has no clear features.
items.html: If the pointed region is a featureless background or too small to extract useful information, the pixel-aware embedding stays low and contributes little. The model falls back on text, defeating the purpose.

items.b: Two-stage training freezes the wrong modules.
items.html: If stage one training is too strong, the base model's weights become inflexible; stage two cannot refine them. LoRA (a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that learns a small correction on top of frozen weights) helps, because it learns new corrections without trying to change the old weights themselves. But only if the base model was not overfit in stage one—if it memorized spurious patterns, no correction layer can fix it.

items.b: Done right: use high-quality masks and multi-stage training.
items.html: Pixel-level annotations must be accurate and large-scale; the two-stage procedure separates learning motion skills from learning pixel-to-action links, so neither interferes with the other.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot control task: a simulated robot arm reaching to pick objects in a cluttered bin. Train a baseline model on text instructions only. Then train PixelVLA on the same task but add random point or box prompts to the training data (e.g., mark the target object's location on 30% of episodes). At test time, a human provides a visual prompt (point to the target), and measure the pick success rate for each model.
demo.metric_eq: Success rate = (number of correct picks) / (total attempts). Improvement = (PixelVLA success rate) - (text-only success rate).
demo.closing: The demo is clear if PixelVLA's success rate jumps visibly in cluttered scenes when a visual prompt is given, while text-only mode stays low—showing that humans can now steer the robot by pointing, not just talking.
